title: ML Systems in Production
tagline: Getting a model to 95% accuracy is 10% of the work — keeping it reliable in production is the other 90%.

sections.content:
You have spent weeks collecting data, engineering features, tuning hyperparameters, and finally — your model achieves 95% accuracy on the held-out test set. Celebration is warranted. But here is the uncomfortable truth that most introductory courses do not tell you: **that moment is roughly 10% of the total engineering effort**. The remaining 90% is building the infrastructure around the model — the pipelines, serving systems, monitoring, retraining loops, and governance frameworks that transform a research artifact into a reliable, trustworthy production service.

This gap is why the field of **MLOps** (Machine Learning Operations) exists. MLOps borrows from DevOps — continuous integration, deployment automation, observability — and adds concerns unique to ML: data versioning, experiment tracking, feature consistency, and the silent degradation that happens when the real world drifts away from the world your model was trained on. A software bug tends to be loud — an exception is thrown, a service crashes. An ML model degrading due to data drift is quiet — it just starts returning confidently wrong answers, and nobody notices for days or weeks.

This chapter covers the full lifecycle of a production ML system from end to end: **data pipelines** that reliably compute features, **feature stores** that prevent training-serving inconsistency, **model registries** that version every experiment, **serving infrastructure** that handles real traffic at scale, **drift detection** that catches silent degradation early, **safe deployment patterns** like shadow mode and canary releases, and **evaluation frameworks** that measure what actually matters in the real world. We will go deep on each component, examine the failure modes, and build the mental model you need to design or reason about any ML system.

A quick map of where we are going: (1) the overall system architecture and why each component exists, (2) data pipelines — the foundation, (3) feature stores and the training-serving skew problem, (4) experiment tracking and model registries, (5) serving infrastructure and latency engineering, (6) model drift — types, detection, and response, (7) safe deployment patterns, (8) production evaluation beyond offline accuracy, and (9) the organizational patterns that make MLOps work at scale.

sections.title: A Commercial Airline — Not Just the Plane
sections.content:
When you board a flight, you are trusting far more than the aircraft's engines. You are trusting the **weather data pipeline** (continuous ingestion of atmospheric readings from thousands of sensors), the **flight planning system** (feature engineering over that raw data — wind vectors, turbulence indices, optimised routing), the **maintenance registry** (every past inspection, part replacement, and anomaly — the model's training history), the **air traffic control serving layer** (real-time decisions based on live data), and the **monitoring and alerting system** (cockpit instrumentation that immediately flags deviation from safe parameters).

The plane's engines are the ML model: critically important, but useless without the surrounding system. An airline that invested everything in building the world's best engine but skipped maintenance records, real-time monitoring, and weather data integration would be terrifying to fly in. The same logic applies to ML in production.

There is one more important parallel: **silent failure modes**. An engine can run slightly rough for hours before a catastrophic failure. An ML model can make subtly wrong predictions for weeks before anyone notices — because there is no crash, no exception, no alert. The model just quietly drifts from reality. This is why **observability** — knowing the health of your system in real time — is not optional.

sections.title: Data Pipelines — The Foundation Everything Depends On
sections.content:
Every ML system starts with data, and the reliability of your data pipeline determines the ceiling of everything downstream. Raw data arrives from databases, event streams, third-party APIs, user activity logs, and IoT sensors. Before any of it can feed a model, it must be **cleaned** (handle nulls, outliers, corrupt records), **validated** (assert schema expectations, range constraints, referential integrity), **transformed** (compute derived features, normalise, encode categoricals), and **delivered** on time (handle late-arriving data gracefully).

Data pipelines are typically structured as **DAGs (Directed Acyclic Graphs)** — tasks with explicit dependencies, orchestrated by tools like **Apache Airflow**, **Prefect**, or **Dagster**. Airflow represents pipelines as Python code, schedules runs on a cron-like calendar, and provides a web UI for monitoring task health and viewing historical runs. Prefect takes a more Pythonic, code-first approach with dynamic task execution. Dagster emphasises data assets and lineage tracking, making it easy to understand what data each step produces and consumes.

**What can go wrong in data pipelines — and frequently does:**

**Late-arriving data** is when event records arrive after the pipeline's processing window. A purchase made at 11:58 PM might not appear in the database until 12:03 AM — after the midnight batch job ran. Naive pipelines miss these records. Solutions include watermarking (accept late records up to N hours after the window closes) and reprocessing windows after a grace period.

**Schema drift** happens when upstream data sources change without notice. A new column appears, an existing column changes type, an enum gains a new value. Pipelines should validate the schema of every batch with explicit expectations (tools like **Great Expectations** or **dbt tests**) and fail loudly — not silently skip records — when violations occur.

**Idempotency** is the property that running a pipeline step multiple times produces the same result as running it once. This is crucial because pipelines fail and need to be retried. A non-idempotent pipeline might double-count events or produce inconsistent feature values on retry.

**Data lineage** — knowing exactly which raw records contributed to which feature values and which model training run — is essential for debugging, auditing, and compliance. Modern tools track lineage automatically, creating a graph from raw source to prediction.

sections.title: Feature Stores — Eliminating the Training-Serving Skew Problem
sections.content:
**Training-serving skew** is one of the most common and insidious causes of production ML failures. It happens when the features computed during training differ — even slightly — from those computed during serving. The model was trained on one version of reality and is being asked to predict on a different one.

Imagine you train a fraud detection model. During training, you compute a feature: `transactions_last_7_days` by querying a historical database with a particular SQL window function. During serving, an engineer writes a slightly different aggregation in the application layer — maybe they use a rolling 7-day window anchored to the current UTC day rather than the event timestamp. Now the feature has subtly different semantics. The model receives inputs unlike anything in its training distribution and produces unreliable predictions — but no error is thrown, and debugging is extremely difficult.

A **feature store** solves this by establishing a **single source of truth for feature computation logic**. The same code runs for both the training path (historical batch computation over past data) and the serving path (real-time computation for live requests). It has two key components:

**Offline store**: A columnar database (Hive, BigQuery, Redshift) optimised for bulk reads of historical feature values. Used to generate training datasets by joining feature values from the correct historical timestamps — a technique called **point-in-time joins**, which prevent future data leakage into training.

**Online store**: A low-latency key-value store (Redis, DynamoDB, Cassandra) that holds the latest feature values for each entity (user, product, session). The serving API queries this to assemble the feature vector for a real-time prediction in single-digit milliseconds.

The feature store also provides **feature reuse**: once you compute a feature for one model, any other model can use it. This prevents redundant computation and ensures consistency across the model portfolio.

Tools in this space: **Feast** (open source, widely adopted), **Tecton** (managed, enterprise-grade), **Vertex AI Feature Store** (Google Cloud native), **Databricks Feature Store** (integrates with MLflow). Choosing among them depends on your cloud environment, real-time latency requirements, and team size.

sections.title: Experiment Tracking and Model Registries — Version Control for ML
sections.content:
Software engineers take version control for granted — every change to code is tracked in git, every release is tagged. ML teams often start without the equivalent, and it creates chaos: 'Which training run produced the model currently in production?' 'What hyperparameters did we use?' 'Was this trained on the v3 or v4 dataset?' 'Why did last week's model perform better?'

**Experiment tracking** answers these questions by logging every training run: the hyperparameters used, the training and validation metrics at each epoch, the dataset version, the code commit hash, the environment (library versions, hardware), and the resulting model artifact. Tools like **MLflow Tracking**, **Weights & Biases (W&B)**, and **Neptune** automatically capture this information and provide dashboards for comparing runs side by side.

A **model registry** is the next layer: a versioned store specifically for models that have passed evaluation and are ready for deployment consideration. Think of it as the 'release branch' in a git workflow. Each registered model version has:
- The model artifact (serialised weights, ONNX file, pickle, SavedModel)
- Evaluation metrics (accuracy, AUC, RMSE, business-relevant KPIs)
- The training run ID (full lineage back to data and code)
- A stage label: Staging, Production, Archived
- Deployment metadata: who approved it, when, for what use case

The deployment workflow becomes: train → evaluate → register → review → promote to Staging → A/B test → promote to Production. At any point, rolling back means demoting the current Production version and promoting the previous one — a single API call. MLflow's model registry, W&B's model management, and SageMaker Model Registry all support this workflow.

**Why reproducibility matters beyond auditing**: If a model makes a consequential decision — a loan denial, a medical flagging, a fraud block — regulators may require you to reproduce the exact prediction months later. Without experiment tracking, this is impossible.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Feature validation rejects malformed inputs before they can corrupt a training dataset or produce garbage predictions at serving time. The `computeFeatures` function is intentionally a pure, side-effect-free function — identical for both the batch training job and the real-time serving handler. The model registry lifecycle (staging → production → archived) mirrors a git release workflow, with explicit promotion and safe rollback to any previously archived version.

sections.title: Serving Infrastructure — Getting Predictions to Users
sections.content:
A trained model sitting in a registry produces no value. It needs to be **served** — exposed as an API that applications can call with a feature vector and receive a prediction back. Serving infrastructure is where ML meets distributed systems engineering, and the performance requirements vary enormously by use case.

**Latency SLA spectrum**: Fraud detection at checkout requires a prediction in under 10ms (p99) — adding 200ms to checkout flow is commercially unacceptable. A content recommendation engine might tolerate 100ms. Batch scoring for overnight reporting can run for hours. Your serving architecture must be designed around the latency budget.

**Model server options**: Rather than deploying a model as raw code, dedicated model servers handle the machinery of loading weights, managing GPU memory, batching requests, and exposing a standardised API:
- **TorchServe**: Official PyTorch serving framework. Supports dynamic batching and model versioning.
- **TensorFlow Serving**: High-performance gRPC/REST server for SavedModels. Battle-tested at Google scale.
- **NVIDIA Triton Inference Server**: Model-format-agnostic (TensorFlow, PyTorch, ONNX, custom). Optimised for GPU inference with sophisticated batching strategies.
- **vLLM**: Purpose-built for large language model serving, with PagedAttention for efficient GPU memory management.

**Dynamic batching** is a key optimisation: rather than processing one request at a time, the server accumulates requests for a short window (e.g., 5ms) and processes a batch together. GPUs are massively parallel — batching a single request is leaving compute on the table. Dynamic batching increases throughput significantly at the cost of slightly increased latency for individual requests.

**Hardware choices**: Neural networks use matrix multiplication, which GPUs excel at. A single A100 GPU can process thousands of inference requests per second for typical models. For smaller models or strict latency requirements, CPUs (with quantisation and ONNX Runtime) may be preferable — no GPU spin-up latency, cheaper to run, lower operational complexity. The decision is driven by model size, latency budget, throughput requirement, and cost.

**A/B testing infrastructure**: The serving layer must support routing a fraction of traffic to a challenger model while the champion handles the rest — all in a way that is deterministic (the same user always sees the same model in a given experiment window), auditable, and instantly rollback-able.

sections.title: Model Drift — The Silent Killer of Production Accuracy
sections.content:
A model does not decay by itself. The world decays around it. **Model drift** is the gradual or sudden degradation of model performance as the statistical properties of real-world data diverge from the training data distribution. It is the most important operational concern in a mature ML system, and it is almost always silent.

There are two distinct types that are important to understand separately:

**Data drift (covariate shift)** means the distribution of input features X changes, but the relationship between X and the target Y remains the same. Example: a model trained on web purchases from 2022 sees a new cohort of mobile-first users in 2024. The age distribution shifts younger, the purchase categories shift toward different products. The model's feature weights were learned on a different population — predictions degrade even though the underlying patterns (what correlates with purchase likelihood) have not changed. Retraining on fresh data usually fixes this.

**Concept drift** is more fundamental: the relationship between features and labels itself changes. A fraud detection model learned that pattern A (rapid cross-country transactions) is fraudulent. Fraudsters observe this and adopt pattern B instead. The feature distribution may look similar, but the semantic mapping has changed. Even a perfectly fresh training set would not help unless it contains enough examples of the new pattern. This requires active feedback loops and sometimes model architecture changes.

**Label shift** (prior probability shift) is a third type: the marginal distribution of labels changes. If your fraud rate was 0.1% during training and spikes to 2% in a new market, a model calibrated for 0.1% base rate will dramatically underestimate fraud probability.

**How to detect drift before it causes problems:**

The gold standard is monitoring actual model accuracy — but this requires **ground truth labels** promptly. In fraud detection, you get chargebacks within days. In a loan default model, you wait months. The monitoring strategy must account for this label latency.

For feature-level monitoring, you do not need labels. Common metrics:
- **Population Stability Index (PSI)**: Compares binned distributions. PSI < 0.1 = stable; 0.1–0.25 = investigate; > 0.25 = significant drift, action required.
- **KL divergence / Jensen-Shannon divergence**: Information-theoretic measures of distribution distance.
- **Kolmogorov-Smirnov test**: Non-parametric statistical test for whether two samples come from the same distribution.
- **Wasserstein distance**: Measures the 'earth-moving cost' to transform one distribution into another — intuitive and well-suited for continuous features.

For output monitoring (even without labels): watch the distribution of predicted probabilities or regression values. If your fraud model suddenly starts predicting high probability for 30% of transactions instead of the usual 0.5%, something has changed.

The operational response to detected drift typically follows a ladder: alert → investigate root cause (data issue? genuine distribution shift?) → trigger retraining → validate new model → deploy via canary.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The PSI function bins both distributions into equal-width bins, computes the proportion in each bin, then applies the PSI formula: sum over bins of (actual - expected) * ln(actual/expected). This is similar to KL divergence but symmetric. The output distribution monitor provides a label-free signal: if the model suddenly starts predicting very different scores on average, something has changed — even before any ground truth labels are available.

sections.title: Safe Deployment Patterns — Controlling the Blast Radius
sections.content:
Deploying a new model to 100% of production traffic immediately is like pushing untested code to production with no rollback plan. The ML equivalent of a staged deployment uses several patterns that progressively expose the new model while limiting risk.

**Shadow mode (dark launch)**: The new model runs alongside the champion, receiving the same requests and computing predictions — but those predictions are **not served to users**. Instead, they are logged to a database. Engineers can then compare the new model's outputs to the champion's offline, computing metrics, checking for anomalies, and building confidence in the new model's behaviour. Zero risk to users; the cost is the extra compute. Shadow mode is the right choice when you are uncertain whether the new model is ready and cannot afford to expose users to potentially worse predictions.

**Canary deployment**: Once shadow mode looks promising, route a small slice of live traffic — typically 1-5% — to the new model. Real users receive predictions from the new model; business metrics (click-through rate, conversion, return rate) and technical metrics (latency, error rate) are monitored. If metrics are acceptable, traffic is gradually shifted: 1% → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%. At any point, rollback is immediate — re-route traffic back to the champion. Canary deployment finds problems that shadow mode cannot: user behaviour reactions, real business impact, edge cases in the production data distribution that were under-represented in evaluation.

**A/B testing**: More rigorous than a canary, A/B tests deliberately assign users to control (champion) or treatment (new model) groups and measure causal impact on business metrics with statistical significance. The test runs long enough to account for novelty effects and weekly seasonality. A/B tests answer 'does this model actually improve the metric we care about?' — which offline accuracy cannot tell you.

**Blue-green deployment**: Maintain two identical production environments (blue = current champion, green = new model). When the new model is ready, switch the load balancer to route all traffic to green. If problems arise, switching back to blue takes seconds. This works well when canary granularity is not needed and instant rollback is paramount.

**Rollback strategy**: Every model deployment should have a documented rollback procedure: which model version to revert to, who has authority to initiate rollback, what monitoring threshold triggers automatic rollback, and how to verify rollback is complete. This is not an afterthought — it should be built into the deployment automation.

sections.mermaid:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Shadow: Deploy new model
    Shadow --> Canary: Shadow looks good
    Shadow --> Registry: Shadow shows issues
    Canary --> FullTraffic: Metrics pass gradually
    Canary --> Champion: Rollback triggered
    FullTraffic --> [*]: New model is champion
    Champion --> [*]: Old champion remains
sections.caption: Safe deployment state machine: shadow mode first (zero user risk), then canary (small real traffic), then full promotion. Issues at any stage trigger rollback to the previous champion.

sections.title: Production Evaluation — Measuring What Actually Matters
sections.content:
Offline accuracy on a test set is a necessary but not sufficient measure of model quality. In production, you need a layered evaluation strategy that answers questions at multiple levels of abstraction.

**Offline metrics** (the starting point): Accuracy, AUC-ROC, precision/recall, RMSE, MAE — computed on held-out test sets. These are fast to compute, reproducible, and useful for comparing candidate models. But they assume the test set distribution matches production, which is rarely perfectly true. They also measure what the model can do, not what it actually does in the system.

**Slice-based evaluation** (catching hidden failures): Aggregate accuracy hides subgroup performance problems. A loan approval model might achieve 88% overall accuracy but only 72% on applicants in a specific demographic — a serious fairness issue and often a regulatory violation. **Slice-based evaluation** computes metrics (accuracy, AUC, RMSE, calibration error) for every meaningful subgroup: age range, geography, device type, account age, product category. Tools like **TensorFlow Model Analysis (TFMA)** and **Fairlearn** automate slice computation and visualisation. The discipline of finding and monitoring slices is sometimes called **model cards** — a structured documentation of performance across dimensions.

**Calibration**: A model might rank examples correctly (high AUC) but assign probabilities that do not match reality. A fraud model predicting 80% probability for an event that happens 20% of the time is miscalibrated. This matters enormously for decision-making: thresholds, risk scoring, and expected value calculations all depend on well-calibrated probabilities. **Calibration curves** (reliability diagrams) and the **Expected Calibration Error (ECE)** quantify this. **Platt scaling** and **isotonic regression** are common post-hoc calibration methods.

**Online A/B test metrics** (the ultimate arbiters): Business metrics — revenue per user, engagement rate, return rate, churn — measure whether the model actually improves the outcome that matters. These are the hardest to move and the most important. An ML team that improves AUC from 0.92 to 0.95 but sees no change in business metrics has not delivered value. Conversely, a small AUC improvement that translates to 0.5% revenue lift on a $100M business is worth $500K/year.

**Latency SLAs as a model constraint**: If your model's p99 inference latency violates the SLA, no amount of accuracy improvement matters — the predictions arrive too late. Monitoring latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99) alongside accuracy is essential. In many production systems, a model that is slightly less accurate but twice as fast is the better business choice.

sections.title: Organizational Patterns and MLOps Maturity
sections.content:
ML systems do not fail only for technical reasons. Many failures are organizational: unclear ownership of model quality, no process for retraining, no escalation path when drift is detected, and models that 'belong' to one team but whose outputs affect many others.

**MLOps maturity levels** describe how much of the ML lifecycle is automated:

**Level 0 — Manual**: Data scientists train models in notebooks, export artifacts manually, and deploy via ad-hoc scripts. Each deployment is a unique, stressful event. No monitoring. Retraining happens when someone notices performance has degraded. This describes most teams in the early stages of ML adoption.

**Level 1 — ML pipeline automation**: Training is automated as a pipeline (Airflow/Prefect DAG). Models are registered in a registry. Continuous training triggers run on a schedule or on data triggers. Monitoring dashboards exist. Deployment is still somewhat manual but follows a documented process.

**Level 2 — Full CI/CD for ML**: New code changes to model pipelines trigger automated training, evaluation, and deployment. A new model is only promoted if it passes automated quality gates (accuracy thresholds, calibration checks, latency benchmarks, slice performance). Rollback is automated when monitoring thresholds are violated. This level requires significant investment but enables teams to safely iterate on models as fast as software teams ship code.

**The ML platform team**: At scale, a dedicated platform team builds and maintains the feature store, experiment tracking infrastructure, model registry, serving infrastructure, and monitoring dashboards. They abstract away the infrastructure complexity so data scientists can focus on modelling. Without this investment, every ML team rebuilds the same infrastructure from scratch, inefficiently and inconsistently.

**Model governance and compliance**: Regulated industries (finance, healthcare, insurance) require documentation of training data lineage, model decision auditing, fairness assessments, and sometimes human review of model decisions. Building auditability into the system from the start — not as an afterthought — is dramatically cheaper than retrofitting it. This means capturing: what data was used to train the model, what evaluation it passed, who approved it for deployment, and for consequential predictions, the feature values that drove each decision.

**The hidden cost of technical debt in ML systems**: ML technical debt differs from software technical debt in one crucial way — it accrues silently and degrades model quality rather than developer velocity. The seminal 2015 Google paper *'Machine Learning: The High-Interest Credit Card of Technical Debt'* identified patterns like **undeclared consumers** (other models depending on your features without you knowing), **correction cascades** (model A corrects for model B's errors, so fixing B breaks A), and **feedback loops** (model predictions influence future training data). These ML-specific debt patterns require architectural discipline — clean interfaces, explicit dependencies, and regular audits — to keep under control.

**Interview and production insight — the offline-online gap**: When asked why a model with 95% offline accuracy underperforms in production, the canonical answers are: (1) **training-serving skew** — features computed differently at train vs. serve time; (2) **data drift** — production distribution has shifted since training; (3) **label leakage** — the offline evaluation inadvertently used information not available at prediction time (e.g., aggregating statistics that include the target event); (4) **feedback loops** — the model's predictions change user behaviour, which changes future training data in a way that degrades the original signal. These four categories cover the vast majority of offline-online gaps seen in practice. The fix always starts with instrumenting the serving pipeline to log actual feature values and comparing them against training data.

items: **MLOps treats ML as a software engineering discipline**: every model needs versioning, CI/CD, monitoring, and runbooks — a model without this infrastructure will silently degrade and is unreliable for production use.

**Feature stores prevent training-serving skew** by encoding feature computation logic once and using it for both historical training batches (offline store) and real-time serving (online store) — the single most impactful architectural pattern in production ML.

**Model drift is the primary operational concern**: data drift (input distribution changes) and concept drift (feature-label relationship changes) cause silent accuracy loss. Proactively monitor feature distributions with PSI and KL divergence before accuracy metrics degrade.

**Model registries provide version control for artifacts**: every training run should log hyperparameters, dataset version, evaluation metrics, and code commit hash. Deployment pulls from the registry; rollback is a single promotion operation.

**Safe deployment uses layered exposure**: shadow mode first (zero user risk, full logging), then canary (small real traffic with business metric monitoring), then gradual traffic increase to 100%. Every deployment must have a tested rollback procedure.

**Offline accuracy is necessary but not sufficient**: slice-based evaluation catches hidden fairness failures; calibration checks whether predicted probabilities match reality; online A/B test business metrics are the ultimate judge of model value.

**MLOps maturity scales from manual (Level 0) to full CI/CD (Level 2)**: teams should invest progressively in automated training pipelines, model registries, monitoring dashboards, and eventually fully automated retraining and deployment based on quality gates.

quiz.question: What is the primary problem that a feature store solves?
options: It stores raw training data in a format optimised for GPU access
It eliminates training-serving skew by ensuring the same feature computation logic runs for both training and real-time serving
It provides a key-value cache for model weights to reduce loading time
It manages hyperparameter search across distributed training workers
quiz.explanation: Training-serving skew occurs when features are computed with slightly different logic at training time versus serving time, causing the model to receive inputs unlike those it learned from. A feature store defines feature computation once and uses it for both the offline training batch (offline store) and the real-time serving lookup (online store), guaranteeing consistency.

quiz.question: What distinguishes concept drift from data drift?
options: Concept drift refers to the input feature distribution changing; data drift refers to label distribution changing
Concept drift means the feature-to-label relationship has changed; data drift means input feature distributions have shifted while the relationship is unchanged
Concept drift only affects regression models; data drift only affects classification models
Concept drift is detectable without labels; data drift requires ground truth to detect
quiz.explanation: Data drift (covariate shift) means the distribution of input features X has changed but the underlying relationship P(Y|X) is the same — retraining on fresh data usually fixes it. Concept drift means P(Y|X) itself has changed — the semantic relationship between features and labels has shifted. For example, fraud patterns that change as fraudsters adapt is concept drift; a new user cohort with different age distribution is data drift.

quiz.question: In shadow mode deployment, what happens to the new model's predictions?
options: They are served to 1% of users to test real-world impact with minimal risk
They are computed and logged but never served to users, enabling safe offline comparison against the champion
They are served only to internal employees before external rollout
They are stored in a queue and served during off-peak hours to reduce load
quiz.explanation: Shadow mode runs the new model in parallel with the champion. Real-user predictions still come entirely from the champion model. The new model's outputs are logged to a data store where engineers compare them offline — checking for anomalies, measuring disagreement rates, and building confidence. Zero user-facing risk, but the extra compute cost is real.

quiz.question: What does a Population Stability Index (PSI) value of 0.32 indicate?
options: The feature distribution is stable and no action is needed
There is moderate drift worth monitoring but not yet acting on
There is significant drift — action such as retraining or root cause investigation is required
The feature has been removed from the model and can be ignored
quiz.explanation: PSI thresholds: < 0.1 = stable (no action); 0.1–0.25 = moderate drift (investigate); > 0.25 = significant drift (action required — typically trigger retraining, alert on-call, and investigate the upstream data source). A PSI of 0.32 is well above the 0.25 threshold, indicating a meaningful distribution shift.

quiz.question: Why is slice-based model evaluation important in production ML?
options: It speeds up evaluation by only testing a random subset of the evaluation data
It reveals subgroup performance failures that aggregate metrics hide, enabling detection of fairness issues and weak spots
It reduces overfitting by training the model on different data slices simultaneously
It partitions model weights into slices for faster parallel inference
quiz.explanation: A model with 90% overall accuracy might have 70% accuracy on a specific demographic — a serious fairness and potentially legal issue invisible in aggregate numbers. Slice-based evaluation computes metrics (accuracy, AUC, calibration) separately for each meaningful subgroup (age group, geography, device type, language) and is the standard method for fairness analysis and finding weak spots in model coverage.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a model registry in an MLOps workflow?
options: To store user prediction requests for GDPR compliance and auditing
To provide a versioned store of trained model artifacts and metadata enabling reproducibility, staged promotion, and safe rollback
To register new feature definitions before they can be used in training
To manage API rate limits and authentication keys for model serving endpoints
quiz.explanation: A model registry stores versioned model artifacts (weights, configs) alongside training metadata (dataset version, hyperparameters, evaluation metrics, code commit). Models move through stages: staging → production → archived. This enables comparing model versions, reproducing any past model, deploying a specific version, and rolling back instantly if a new model underperforms — analogous to tagged releases in a code repository.

quiz.question: What is model calibration, and why does it matter in production?
options: Calibration is the process of tuning hyperparameters before deployment
A calibrated model's predicted probabilities match empirical frequencies — a model predicting 80% fraud should be wrong about 20% of the time
Calibration refers to matching model latency to the serving SLA
A calibrated model is one that has been tested on data from all geographic regions
quiz.explanation: Calibration measures whether predicted probabilities correspond to actual event frequencies. If a model says 'fraud probability = 0.8' for a set of transactions, roughly 80% of those transactions should actually be fraud. Miscalibrated models produce incorrect probability estimates even when ranking is accurate (high AUC). Calibration matters for risk scoring, threshold setting, and expected value calculations.

quiz.question: In canary deployment for ML models, what is the typical progression of traffic routing?
options: Deploy to 100% of traffic immediately, then roll back if issues arise
Route a small percentage (e.g. 1-5%) to the new model, monitor metrics, and gradually increase traffic as confidence grows
Deploy only to users who opt in to beta features, then release broadly
Route traffic on alternate days between old and new model for two weeks
quiz.explanation: Canary deployment starts with a small slice of traffic (1-5%) to the new model while the champion handles the rest. Business metrics (conversion, latency, error rate) are monitored closely. If metrics remain healthy, traffic is gradually shifted: 1% → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%. At any point, rollback is instant — re-routing traffic to the champion limits blast radius if issues emerge.

quiz.question: What is 'label leakage' and why does it cause the offline-online accuracy gap?
options: Label leakage is when training labels are accidentally written to the production database
Label leakage is when offline evaluation uses features that contain future information unavailable at real prediction time, inflating offline metrics
Label leakage is when the same label is used to train two different models simultaneously
Label leakage is when prediction labels from one model are passed as features to another
quiz.explanation: Label leakage occurs when a feature in the training/evaluation dataset inadvertently encodes information about the outcome that would not be available at real prediction time. For example, including the timestamp of a fraud resolution event as a feature, or computing a user-level aggregation that includes the target transaction. The model learns to exploit this signal, achieving high offline accuracy but failing in production where that information genuinely does not exist yet.

quiz.question: Which component of MLOps infrastructure addresses the 'late-arriving data' problem in data pipelines?
options: The model registry, by storing multiple model versions to handle different data states
Watermarking and grace-period reprocessing windows in pipeline orchestration
The feature store online store, which only accepts real-time data
Shadow mode deployment, which buffers predictions until data arrives
quiz.explanation: Late-arriving data occurs when event records appear in the source database after the pipeline processing window has closed. Watermarking defines how late records are accepted (e.g., up to 2 hours after the window closes). Grace-period reprocessing reruns the pipeline after a delay to include records that arrived late. Pipeline orchestrators like Apache Airflow and Apache Flink have built-in support for these patterns.
